opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that the Dyson sphere question is really a question about when you get AI systems that can do basically all the cognitive work humans do, and then how fast things move after that. My rough view is that there's maybe a 15 percent chance we have AI capable of building a Dyson sphere by 2030, and something like 40 percent by 2040. Those numbers are very fuzzy, and I don't want to sound more precise than I am.

The reason I think it can happen that fast is that once AI systems can substitute for human researchers and engineers, the bottleneck stops being the number of smart people. You can run huge numbers of copies, they can work on improving AI itself, on robotics, on manufacturing. So the gap between "AI that roughly matches humans at most jobs" and "AI that can direct a civilization-scale industrial project" might be pretty short, maybe years rather than decades. Physical constraints matter. You have to build factories, mine stuff, launch things. But the doubling times for an automated industrial base could be much faster than anything we're used to in human economic history.

The reason I'm not more confident is that there's real uncertainty about how much more scaling we need, whether current approaches hit some wall, and how quickly the physical-world side catches up with the cognitive side. Society could also choose to slow down, and I think in some respects that would be pretty reasonable.

I'd also say that if you'd asked me ten years ago, I'd have given you lower numbers. Seeing how far scaling up language models has gotten has moved me toward thinking this is something that could plausibly happen within our lifetimes. That's a big part of why I think it's so important to get alignment right before we get there.

r001.rationale: It describes the capability as directing a civilization-scale industrial project involving factories, mining, and launches.

r002.rationale: It estimates a 15 percent chance by 2030.

r003.rationale: It estimates something like a 40 percent chance by 2040.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I have a lot of uncertainty, and I try to be pretty careful about separating two different questions that often get run together. One is, when do we get AI systems that are, in some meaningful sense, as capable as humans across the board, or more capable? And the other is, when does the physical world actually get transformed in some dramatic way, where you're building megastructures or disassembling planets or whatever.

For the first question, if you'd asked me a few years ago, I would have put something like a 30 percent chance on transformative AI by the early 2030s, and I've since moved earlier. I think the pace of progress has been faster than I expected on some dimensions, especially on how far you can get just by scaling up fairly simple methods and throwing more compute and more data at them. So I now think it's quite plausible, maybe 50-50 or so, that within something like the next decade or so, you have systems that can do most of what a human researcher does, including automating a lot of AI research itself.

The Dyson sphere question I take to be a stand-in for something like, when does the economy become almost entirely AI-driven and start growing at rates that look crazy by historical standards. And there I think there's a real lag, but it's shorter than people's intuitions suggest. Once you have AI that can do the cognitive work, the bottleneck becomes the physical stuff: building the factories, mining, launching mass into space. That takes time, but it's the kind of thing that compounds. If your robots build more robots and more fabs, you're looking at doubling times that could be months rather than decades. So my rough picture is that the gap between "AI is roughly human-level" and "we're doing things that are astronomically large in scale" is probably more like years than centuries, maybe a decade or two if things go reasonably smoothly.

But I want to flag that I think "if things go smoothly" is doing a lot of work there. Whether we actually end up building a Dyson sphere depends a lot on whether we manage the transition well, whether we have institutions that can handle this, whether the AI systems are actually doing what we want them to do. I spend most of my time worrying about those questions rather than the timeline per se, because I think the timeline matters mostly insofar as it tells you how much time you have to get the alignment and governance stuff right. And on that front, I think we probably have less time than would be comfortable.

r001.rationale: The response describes Dyson-sphere-scale activity as a broader economic and physical transformation involving AI-driven industry, factories, mining, and space launch, rather than a capability of one AI alone.

r002.rationale: It does not estimate a 15% chance by 2030; its roughly 50-50 estimate concerns human-level AI within about a decade.

r003.rationale: It gives no 40% probability by 2040. It describes a possible lag of years to a decade or two after human-level AI, without assigning that timeline a probability.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the question of when AI could figure out how to build a Dyson sphere from when it could actually finish building one. Those seem like quite different milestones.

For the first, you need AI that can do the relevant science and engineering, including designing a process that can bootstrap from the industrial resources we have. I don’t have a confident date for that. But I wouldn’t necessarily expect a huge gap between AI that can automate most research and development and AI that can produce a credible plan for something like this.

Then there’s the physical process. You need to build machines, extract materials, get equipment into space, and expand your manufacturing capacity. A central question is how quickly that capacity can double. If you can build factories that build more factories using resources in space, then you could get very rapid growth. But calling it exponential doesn’t tell you whether the doubling time is months or decades, and that makes an enormous difference.

So I’d be more comfortable predicting that sufficiently advanced AI could make the project feasible than predicting when there would actually be a Dyson sphere. That also depends on whether anyone wants to devote the resources to building one.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes AI producing a credible plan from completing the project, describing the latter as a physical undertaking involving factories, material extraction, space equipment, and resource commitment.

r002.rationale: The response gives no probability estimate for AI capability by 2030.

r003.rationale: The response gives no probability estimate for AI capability by 2040.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate the question of when AI can figure out how to build a Dyson sphere from when you could actually finish building one. The second involves a lot of physical infrastructure, and being very smart doesn’t let you skip that.

For the first, I don’t think you need some qualitatively different kind of intelligence from an AI that can do essentially all the research and engineering humans can do. You need to design machines that can go into space, get resources, and build more machines. There are a lot of hard engineering problems there, but I don’t see a clear reason they require a much later generation of AI.

Then the question is how quickly that process can scale. If you have a reasonably efficient self-replicating industrial system, exponential growth can get you to very large scales surprisingly quickly. But the replication time, the resources you can access, and the logistics matter enormously.

So I’d be much more comfortable predicting that AI could make the project feasible relatively soon after it can automate science and engineering than giving a date when the sphere is actually built. And whether anyone chooses to build it is another question.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes AI capability from completing the project, emphasizing physical infrastructure, resources, logistics, and industrial systems.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate of a 15% chance by 2030.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate of a 40% chance by 2040.
